description: Covers the full set of pointer-rewiring techniques for linked lists: full and partial reversal, dummy-node scaffolding, merging and partitioning, deep copying with auxiliary pointers, and building composite structures like LRU caches. The unifying constraint is that you cannot index randomly — everything is done by carefully re-pointing next references in O(1) extra space.
important_details: Draw prev / curr / next on paper before writing any reversal code — pointer-order bugs are the dominant failure mode.
A dummy node placed before the head removes every 'what if the head itself changes' special case in insertion, deletion, merging, and partitioning.
Always save curr.next BEFORE overwriting curr.next, or the rest of the list becomes unreachable.
Recursive solutions are shorter but cost O(n) call-stack space — know the iterative version, since the O(1)-space requirement is the standard follow-up.
This pattern composes heavily with Fast & Slow Pointers: most Medium/Hard list problems are 'find a position' plus 'rewire around it'.
other_relevant_details: Linked list questions are disproportionately common in phone screens because they test pointer discipline rather than algorithmic insight. The highest-value practice is writing reverse, merge, and remove-with-dummy from memory until they are automatic, since almost every harder problem decomposes into those three.

variations.description: Re-point each node's next to its predecessor using three tracking pointers, producing a fully reversed list in one O(n) pass with O(1) space.
important_details: prev starts as null — it becomes the new tail's next, correctly terminating the reversed list.
The loop ends when curr is null, at which point prev is the new head. Returning curr or head instead of prev is the classic mistake.
The recursive version reverses the sublist after head, then sets head.next.next = head and head.next = null — elegant but O(n) stack space.
Be ready to state both versions and their space trade-off without being asked.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) iterative, O(n) recursive.

problems.name: Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups

variations.variation: Reverse a Sublist (Positions m to n)
variations.description: Reverse only a bounded segment of the list while leaving the prefix and suffix intact, requiring careful reconnection at both seams.
important_details: Use a dummy node so that a segment starting at position 1 needs no special handling.
Track four conceptual pointers: the node before the segment, the segment's original head (which becomes its tail), the segment's new head, and the node after the segment.
The head-insertion approach is cleaner than a full reverse-then-reconnect: repeatedly move the node after curr to the front of the segment.
Verify with a 2-node list and with m == n, both of which expose off-by-one seam errors.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups

variations.description: Repeatedly reverse every consecutive block of k nodes, leaving any final partial block untouched, and stitching each reversed block back to the previous one.
important_details: Before reversing a block, walk ahead k nodes to confirm a full block exists; if fewer remain, stop and leave them as-is.
Maintain a groupPrev pointer to the node preceding the current block, and compute groupNext (the node after the block) before reversing.
After reversing, the block's original first node becomes its last — update groupPrev to that node for the next iteration.
The recursive version is much shorter and is acceptable in most interviews, but note its O(n/k) stack usage.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) — each node is visited a constant number of times. Space: O(1) iterative.

problems.name: Reverse Nodes in Even Length Groups

variations.description: Prepend a placeholder node before the real head so deletion, insertion, and filtering logic never needs a special case for changes at the head.
important_details: Always return dummy.next, never the original head reference, which may no longer be first.
For deleting ALL nodes with a given value, keep a prev pointer and only advance it when the current node survives.
For deleting all nodes that appear more than once (not just extras), you must skip an entire run and link prev directly past it.
Combining a dummy node with a fixed-gap fast pointer gives the one-pass 'remove Nth from end' solution.

problems.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List
Delete Node in a Linked List

variations.description: Weave two sorted lists into one by repeatedly appending whichever head is smaller, using a dummy node and a tail pointer.
important_details: This is merge sort's merge step, but on lists it needs only O(1) extra space because nodes are relinked rather than copied.
After one list is exhausted, attach the remainder of the other in a single assignment — do not loop through it.
Use <= rather than < when comparing to keep the merge stable, which matters if nodes carry extra payload.
Serves as the subroutine for both k-way merging and merge sort on a linked list.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(m + n). Space: O(1).

variations.variation: Merge K Sorted Lists (Heap or Divide & Conquer)
variations.description: Combine k sorted lists either by seeding a min-heap with each list's head (O(N log k)) or by repeatedly merging pairs of lists in a divide-and-conquer tournament (also O(N log k), O(1) space).
important_details: Heap approach: push each list's current head; pop the global minimum, append it, and push its successor.
Divide-and-conquer approach: merge lists pairwise, halving the list count each round — O(1) space and often faster in practice.
Naive sequential merging (merge list 1 with 2, then with 3...) is O(N*k) and is the answer to avoid.
Skip null lists when seeding the heap, or you will get a NullPointerException on the first poll.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(N log k) where N is the total node count. Space: O(k) for the heap approach, O(1) for divide and conquer.

problems.name: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists

variations.description: Split a single list into two or more chains based on a predicate (value threshold, odd/even position, equal part sizes), then reconnect the chains in the required order.
important_details: Build each output chain with its own dummy node and tail pointer, then join them at the end.
CRITICAL: terminate the final chain by setting its tail.next = null, or you create a cycle and the judge hangs.
Order preservation within each partition is usually required — appending to tails rather than heads gives this for free.
For splitting into k equal parts, the first (n mod k) parts get one extra node each.

variations.variation: Sort a Linked List (Merge Sort on Lists)
variations.description: Sort a list in O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space by recursively splitting at the middle (fast/slow) and merging the sorted halves — quicksort is a poor fit because lists lack random access.
important_details: Split using fast/slow, but you must CUT the list: set the node before slow to null, or the recursion never terminates.
Merge sort is preferred over quicksort here because merging lists is O(1) space while partitioning lists is awkward.
The recursive version uses O(log n) stack space; a bottom-up iterative merge sort achieves true O(1) space and is the strict answer to the follow-up.
Insertion sort on a list is O(n^2) but appears as its own easier problem — know both.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log n). Space: O(log n) recursion stack, O(1) for the bottom-up iterative version.

variations.variation: Deep Copy with Auxiliary Pointers (Interleaving Trick)
variations.description: Clone a list whose nodes carry an extra arbitrary pointer, using the O(1)-space interleaving technique: weave copies into the original list, wire the extra pointers by adjacency, then unweave.
important_details: Pass 1: insert each copy immediately after its original, so copy = original.next for every node.
Pass 2: set copy.random = original.random.next — the adjacency makes the mapping free, replacing a HashMap.
Pass 3: unweave the two interleaved lists, restoring the original AND producing the clone.
The HashMap approach (original -> copy) is simpler and O(n) space; the interleaving version is the O(1)-space follow-up interviewers ask for.
Handle null random pointers explicitly in pass 2 or you get a NullPointerException.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) across three passes. Space: O(1) excluding the output, versus O(n) for the HashMap approach.

problems.name: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

variations.variation: Doubly Linked List Design (LRU / LFU Cache)
variations.description: Build a custom doubly linked list paired with a HashMap so that lookup, insertion, and eviction of the least-recently-used entry all run in O(1) — the canonical system-design-flavoured list question.
important_details: HashMap gives O(1) lookup from key to node; the doubly linked list gives O(1) removal and re-insertion because each node knows its predecessor.
Use sentinel head and tail nodes so add and remove never need null checks.
On get: move the node to the front (most recent). On put when at capacity: evict the node just before the tail sentinel.
A singly linked list cannot do this in O(1) — you would need the previous node, which is exactly why the list must be doubly linked.
LFU extends this with a frequency-to-list map plus a minFrequency counter, and is a common Hard follow-up.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(1) for both get and put. Space: O(capacity).

problems.name: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

variations.description: Find where two lists converge, or compare their structure, using length alignment or the two-pass pointer-switching trick that equalizes traversal distance without computing lengths.
important_details: Pointer-switching trick: when pointer A reaches the end, redirect it to headB, and vice versa. Both travel lenA + lenB steps and meet at the intersection (or at null).
The trick works precisely because both pointers cover the same total distance, cancelling out any length difference.
The explicit alternative is: compute both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk in lockstep.
If the lists do not intersect, both pointers become null simultaneously, so the loop terminates correctly with a null return.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(m + n). Space: O(1), versus O(n) for a HashSet of visited nodes.
